claim: FK506 (Tacrolimus) is a potent inhibitor of calcineurin that blocks IL2 production.
source: FK506 (Tacrolimus) is a potent inhibitor of calcineurin that blocks IL2 production and is widely used to prevent transplant rejection and treat autoimmunity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bierer et al., 1990 in the Introduction section

claim: FK506 is widely used to prevent transplant rejection and treat autoimmunity.
source: FK506 (Tacrolimus) is a potent inhibitor of calcineurin that blocks IL2 production and is widely used to prevent transplant rejection and treat autoimmunity.
evidence: Established clinical use referenced in the Abstract and Introduction

claim: FK506 treatment of dendritic cells (FKDC) limits their capacity to stimulate T cell responses.
source: FK506 treatment of dendritic cells (FKDC) limits their capacity to stimulate T cell responses.
evidence: Supported by citations to Woltman et al., 2000; Szabo et al., 2001; Duperrier et al., 2005 and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1A and 1B

claim: FK506 does not prevent DC survival, maturation, or costimulatory molecule expression.
source: FK506 does not prevent DC survival, maturation, or costimulatory molecule expression, suggesting that the limited capacity of FKDC to stimulate T cells may be due to inhibition of calcineurin signaling in the DC.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1C showing phenotype of FK506 treated or untreated DC

claim: DC inhibit T cells by sequestering FK506 and continuously releasing the drug over several days.
source: Instead, we demonstrate that DC inhibit T cells by sequestering FK506 and continuously releasing the drug over several days.
evidence: Demonstrated by FK506 ELISA measurements in Figure 2B showing sustained drug release for 72 hours

claim: T cells encountering FKDC proliferate but fail to upregulate the survival factor bcl-xl and die.
source: T cells encountering FKDC proliferate but fail to upregulate the survival factor bcl-xl and die, and IL2 restores both bcl-xl and survival.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B and 3C showing increased apoptosis and reduced bcl-xl in T cells cultured with FKDC

claim: IL2 restores both bcl-xl and survival in T cells encountering FKDC.
source: T cells encountering FKDC proliferate but fail to upregulate the survival factor bcl-xl and die, and IL2 restores both bcl-xl and survival.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B and 3C showing IL2 supplementation rescues T cell survival and bcl-xl expression

claim: In mice, FKDC act in an antigen-specific manner to inhibit T-cell mediated autoimmune arthritis.
source: In mice, FKDC act in an antigen-specific manner to inhibit T-cell mediated autoimmune arthritis.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4A and 4B showing FKDC-CII but not FKDC-CI protected mice from collagen-induced arthritis

claim: DCs can act as a cellular drug delivery system to target antigen specific T cells.
source: This establishes that DCs can act as a cellular drug delivery system to target antigen specific T cells.
evidence: Inferred from the combined experimental results showing antigen-specific effects of FKDC in vitro and in vivo

claim: FK506 use is limited by side effects including diabetes, hypertension, nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
source: FK506 (Tacrolimus) has a long record of clinical success in preventing transplant rejection and treating autoimmunity, but its use is limited by side effects including diabetes, hypertension, nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity.
evidence: Established clinical knowledge about FK506 side effects

claim: FK506 triggers activated T cell death.
source: Through this mechanism, FK506 inhibits IL2 production (Bierer et al., 1990) and triggers activated T cell death (Horigome et al., 1998; Migita et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Horigome et al., 1998; Migita et al., 1999

claim: FK506 limits the capacity of dendritic cells (DC) to stimulate allogeneic T cell responses in vitro.
source: FK506 also limits the capacity of dendritic cells (DC) to stimulate allogeneic T cell responses in vitro (Woltman et al., 2000; Szabo et al., 2001; Duperrier et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Woltman et al., 2000; Szabo et al., 2001; Duperrier et al., 2005

claim: Rapamycin and mycophenolate inhibit DC maturation.
source: While other immunosuppressants, including rapamycin and mycophenolate, are known to inhibit DC maturation (Hackstein and Thomson, 2004; Popov et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hackstein and Thomson, 2004; Popov et al., 2006

claim: FK506 does not inhibit DC maturation.
source: FK506 does not inhibit DC maturation (Woltman et al., 2000; Szabo et al., 2001; Duperrier et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Woltman et al., 2000; Szabo et al., 2001; Duperrier et al., 2005 and demonstrated in Figure 1C

claim: FKDC were less effective stimulators of allogeneic T cell proliferation than DC despite washing to remove residual drug.
source: Despite washing to remove residual drug from the supernatants, FKDC were less effective stimulators of allogeneic T cell proliferation than DC (Figure 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1A showing reduced T cell proliferation with FKDC

claim: FKDC were markedly less stimulatory than untreated DCs when memory T cell responses to influenza were measured by IFNγ Elispot assay.
source: Similarly, when memory T cell responses to influenza were measured by IFNγ Elispot assay (Albert et al., 1998; Orange et al., 2004), FKDC were found to be markedly less stimulatory than untreated DCs (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1B showing reduced IFNγ spot forming cells with FKDC

claim: DC survival, maturation, expression of MHC and costimulatory molecules were unaffected by FK506 treatment.
source: Moreover, in agreement with previous work (Woltman et al., 2000; Duperrier et al., 2005), DC survival, maturation, expression of MHC and costimulatory molecules were unaffected by FK506 treatment (Figure 1C)
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1C and supported by citations to Woltman et al., 2000; Duperrier et al., 2005

claim: FK506 pretreatment of mature DC for as little as 20 min led to the same level of T cell inhibition as pretreatment for 40 hr.
source: Unexpectedly, FK506 pretreatment of mature DC for as little as 20 min led to the same level of T cell inhibition in the IFNγ Elispot assay as pretreatment for 40 hr (Figure 1D)
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1D showing similar T cell inhibition with different FK506 treatment durations

claim: Maximal 3H-FK506 uptake by Jurkat T cells occurs in only 20 min of FK506 treatment.
source: reminiscent of previous work demonstrating maximal 3H-FK506 uptake by Jurkat T cells in only 20 min of FK506 treatment (Siekierka et al., 1989b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siekierka et al., 1989b

claim: FKDC were poor inducers of T cell IFNγ mRNA responses to influenza.
source: Consistent with the results from Elispot assays, FKDC were poor inducers of T cell IFNγ mRNA responses to influenza (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1E showing reduced IFNγ mRNA induction with FKDC

claim: Combining FKDC with untreated DC inhibited the T cell stimulatory capacity of the untreated DC in a dose dependent manner.
source: Combining FKDC with untreated DC inhibited the T cell stimulatory capacity of the untreated DC in a dose dependent manner (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1E showing dose-dependent inhibition when FKDC are mixed with untreated DC

claim: FKDC supernatants, but not those of untreated DC, were potent inhibitors of IFNγ, IL17A, IL4 and IL2 induction.
source: FKDC supernatants, but not those of untreated DC, were potent inhibitors of IFNγ, IL17A, IL4 and IL2 induction (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1F showing inhibition of multiple cytokines by FKDC supernatants

claim: FKDC produce a T cell inhibitor.
source: Taken together, these data provide strong evidence that FKDC produce a T cell inhibitor.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments in Figure 1 showing inhibitory effects of FKDC and their supernatants

claim: Pretreatment of FKDC with actinomycin, emetine, or brefeldin A prior to FK506 treatment did not affect FKDC secretion of the T cell inhibitor.
source: After washing and co-culture with T cells stimulated with anti-CD3/28, none of these treatments affected FKDC secretion of the T cell inhibitor (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2A showing no effect of transcription, translation, or secretory pathway inhibitors

claim: The inhibitory action of FKDC does not require new gene transcription, translation or translocation through the secretory pathway.
source: To test if the inhibitory action of FKDC requires new gene transcription, translation or translocation through the secretory pathway, FKDC were pretreated with actinomycin, emetine, or brefeldin A prior to FK506 treatment. After washing and co-culture with T cells stimulated with anti-CD3/28, none of these treatments affected FKDC secretion of the T cell inhibitor (Figure 2A).
evidence: Inferred from experimental results in Figure 2A showing no effect of inhibitors of these processes

claim: FK506 was maintained in FKDC supernatants at levels sufficient to block T cell activation for 72 hr after initial washout.
source: FK506 was maintained in the supernatants at levels sufficient to block T cell activation for 72 hr after initial washout (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2B showing FK506 levels measured by ELISA over 4 days

claim: FK506 is the only inhibitor in FKDC supernatants.
source: Next, to assess whether FK506 is the only inhibitor, supernatants were treated with magnetic beads coated with FK-1 antibody that binds with high affinity to FK506 and then immunoadsorbed on a magnetic column. T cells were resuspended in FK-1 depleted or control supernatants and stimulated with anti-CD3/28. Treatment of FKDC supernatants with FK-1 depleted supernatant specifically abolished the inhibitory factor completely (Figure 2C).
evidence: Inferred from complete abolishment of inhibitory activity after FK506 removal in Figure 2C

claim: DCs express several FKBP, with FKBP12 (also known as FKBP1A) being the most robustly expressed.
source: DCs express several FKBP, with FKBP12 (also known as FKBP1A) being the most robustly expressed (Table 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by gene expression profiling data presented in Table 1

claim: FKBP proteins act in concert as an FK506 drug sink in DCs.
source: DCs express several FKBP, with FKBP12 (also known as FKBP1A) being the most robustly expressed (Table 1), suggesting that these proteins act in concert as an FK506 drug sink.
evidence: Speculated based on expression data in Table 1 and known FK506 binding properties

claim: Rapamycin binds FKBP12 with higher affinity than FK506.
source: Rapamycin is another immunomodulatory drug, which binds FKBP12, and it binds FKBP12 with higher affinity than FK506 (FK506 Kd = 0.4 nM, Rapamycin Kd = 0.2 nM) (Bierer et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bierer et al., 1990 with specific Kd values provided

claim: FK506 blocks IL2 cytokine production.
source: Unlike FK506, which blocks IL2 cytokine production, Rapamycin inhibits the downstream effects of IL2R signaling.
evidence: Established mechanism of FK506 action referenced throughout the manuscript

claim: Rapamycin inhibits the downstream effects of IL2R signaling.
source: Unlike FK506, which blocks IL2 cytokine production, Rapamycin inhibits the downstream effects of IL2R signaling.
evidence: Established mechanism of Rapamycin action

claim: Pretreatment with Rapamycin renders Jurkat T cells resistant to FK506 mediated blockade of IL2 induction.
source: The binding of FK506 and Rapamycin to a common intracellular protein was originally demonstrated in Jurkat T cells, which were rendered resistant to FK506 mediated blockade of IL2 induction when pretreated with Rapamycin (Bierer et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bierer et al., 1990

claim: Pretreatment with Rapamycin renders FKDC unable to block IL2 induction in T cells.
source: Similar to the reported results in Jurkat cells, we found that pretreatment with Rapamycin renders FKDC unable to block IL2 induction in T cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 2D showing IL2 induction is restored when DCs are pretreated with Rapamycin before FK506

claim: FKBP12 plays a physiologically relevant role in mediating the action of FKDC on T cell inhibition.
source: This data indicates FKBP12 plays a physiologically relevant role in mediating the action of FKDC on T cell inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from Rapamycin competition experiment in Figure 2D

claim: DCs can absorb significant amounts of FK506, and then release drug into the supernatant in concentrations sufficient to inhibit T cell activation in a sustained manner, for at least 72 hr after a single brief treatment of DCs.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that DCs can absorb significant amounts of FK506, and then release drug into the supernatant in concentrations sufficient to inhibit T cell activation in a sustained manner, for at least 72 hr after a single brief treatment of DCs.
evidence: Demonstrated by multiple experiments in Figure 2, particularly FK506 ELISA measurements in Figure 2B

claim: T cell activation when calcineurin is inhibited leads to antigen specific T cell death.
source: Previous work suggests that T cell activation when calcineurin is inhibited leads to antigen specific T cell death (Vanier and Prud'homme, 1992; Migita et al., 1995, 1997; Horigome et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vanier and Prud'homme, 1992; Migita et al., 1995, 1997; Horigome et al., 1998

claim: There was no difference in the amount of cell death in undivided T cells cultured with FKDC or untreated DC.
source: There was no difference in the amount of cell death in undivided T cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3A and 3B showing annexin V staining of undivided cells

claim: T cells proliferating in response to FKDC were twice as likely to die compared to those stimulated with untreated DC.
source: In contrast, T cells proliferating in response to FKDC were twice as likely to die and IL2 increased survival (Figure 3B)
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B showing increased annexin V staining in divided T cells cultured with FKDC

claim: IL2 increased survival of T cells proliferating in response to FKDC.
source: In contrast, T cells proliferating in response to FKDC were twice as likely to die and IL2 increased survival (Figure 3B)
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B showing reduced annexin V staining when IL2 is added to FKDC cultures

claim: Adding IL2 to T cells stimulated with untreated DC increased cell death consistent with overstimulation of the IL2 pathway and induction of activation induced cell death (AICD).
source: As expected, proliferating T cells stimulated with untreated DC divided, and adding IL2 increased cell death consistent with overstimulation of the IL2 pathway and induction of activation induced cell death (AICD) (Lenardo, 1991).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B and supported by citation to Lenardo, 1991

claim: Fewer proliferating T cells upregulated the survival factor bcl-xl in response to FKDC than untreated DC.
source: Fewer proliferating T cells upregulated the survival factor bcl-xl in response to FKDC than untreated DC (Figure 3C)
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3C showing reduced bcl-xl staining in divided T cells cultured with FKDC

claim: Reduced bcl-xl upregulation in T cells cultured with FKDC suggests cell autonomous (mitochondrial mediated) cell death.
source: Fewer proliferating T cells upregulated the survival factor bcl-xl in response to FKDC than untreated DC (Figure 3C), suggesting cell autonomous (mitochondrial mediated) cell death (Akbar et al., 1996; Hildeman et al., 2002)
evidence: Inferred from bcl-xl data in Figure 3C and supported by citations to Akbar et al., 1996; Hildeman et al., 2002

claim: FK506 sensitizes activated T cells to apoptosis by blocking bcl-xl induction.
source: consistent with reports that FK506 sensitizes activated T cells to apoptosis by blocking bcl-xl induction (Migita et al., 1995, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Migita et al., 1995, 1997

claim: IL2 augments bcl-xl induction and rescues T cells from death.
source: Moreover, we found IL2 augments bcl-xl induction and rescues T cells from death (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3C showing increased bcl-xl staining when IL2 is added to FKDC cultures

claim: IL2 rescues IFNγ production in FKDC activated memory T cells.
source: Furthermore, IL2 rescues IFNγ production in FKDC activated memory T cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3D showing increased IFNγ spot forming cells when IL2 is added to FKDC cultures

claim: Co-culture of T cells with FKDC initiates a program of activation that leads to increased apoptosis.
source: In conclusion, co-culture of T cells with FKDC initiates a program of activation that leads to increased apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments in Figure 3 showing T cell proliferation but increased death with FKDC

claim: Mice infused with FKDC pulsed with CII, but not with CI or untreated DC pulsed with CII, were significantly protected from collagen-induced arthritis as measured by mean arthritis severity score.
source: Mice infused with FKDC pulsed with CII, but not with CI or untreated DC pulsed with CII, were significantly protected as measured by mean arthritis severity score (Figure 4A)
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4A showing reduced arthritis severity scores in FKDC-CII treated mice

claim: Mice infused with FKDC pulsed with CII, but not with CI or untreated DC pulsed with CII, were significantly protected from collagen-induced arthritis as measured by incidence of severe arthritis.
source: Mice infused with FKDC pulsed with CII, but not with CI or untreated DC pulsed with CII, were significantly protected as measured by mean arthritis severity score (Figure 4A) and by incidence of severe arthritis (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4B showing reduced incidence of severe arthritis in FKDC-CII treated mice

claim: Mean arthritis severity scores were highly correlated with radiographic scores (r = 0.97).
source: At day 87 after disease induction, all paws of control mice and mice treated with FKDC-CII or DC-CII were assigned histopathology (Figure 4C) and radiographic (Figure 4D) severity scores, revealing that mean arthritis severity scores were highly correlated with radiographic scores and histopathology severity scores (r = 0.97 and 0.96, respectively).
evidence: Statistical correlation calculated from experimental data comparing clinical, radiographic, and histopathology scores

claim: Mean arthritis severity scores were highly correlated with histopathology severity scores (r = 0.96).
source: At day 87 after disease induction, all paws of control mice and mice treated with FKDC-CII or DC-CII were assigned histopathology (Figure 4C) and radiographic (Figure 4D) severity scores, revealing that mean arthritis severity scores were highly correlated with radiographic scores and histopathology severity scores (r = 0.97 and 0.96, respectively).
evidence: Statistical correlation calculated from experimental data comparing clinical, radiographic, and histopathology scores

claim: Mice treated with FKDC-CII had significantly reduced radiographic severity scores compared to mice treated with DC-CII.
source: Mice treated with FKDC-CII had significantly reduced radiographic (Wilcoxon rank test p<0.05) and histopathology severity scores (Wilcoxon rank test p<0.05) compared to mice treated with DC-CII.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally with statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank test p<0.05) of radiographic data in Figure 4D

claim: Mice treated with FKDC-CII had significantly reduced histopathology severity scores compared to mice treated with DC-CII.
source: Mice treated with FKDC-CII had significantly reduced radiographic (Wilcoxon rank test p<0.05) and histopathology severity scores (Wilcoxon rank test p<0.05) compared to mice treated with DC-CII.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally with statistical analysis (Wilcoxon rank test p<0.05) of histopathology data in Figure 4C

claim: Systemic treatment with FK506 is effective for preventing CIA.
source: Systemic treatment with FK506 is also effective for preventing CIA (Takagishi et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takagishi et al., 1989

claim: Mice treated with 4 mg/kg FK506 do not develop any arthritis.
source: Mice treated with 4 mg/kg FK506 do not develop any arthritis; however mice treated with 1 mg/kg FK506 receive no protection from arthritis.
evidence: Referenced from work by Takagishi et al. described in the manuscript

claim: Mice treated with 1 mg/kg FK506 receive no protection from arthritis.
source: Mice treated with 4 mg/kg FK506 do not develop any arthritis; however mice treated with 1 mg/kg FK506 receive no protection from arthritis.
evidence: Referenced from work by Takagishi et al. described in the manuscript

claim: Mice treated with 2 mg/kg FK506 on day 0–13 led to a 50% reduction in arthritis severity compared to placebo.
source: Mice treated with 2 mg/kg on day 0–13 led to a 50% reduction in arthritis severity compared to placebo.
evidence: Referenced from work by Takagishi et al. described in the manuscript

claim: Serum from mice treated with 2 mg/kg FK506, but not mice treated with FKDC, potently inhibits T cell activation.
source: We found that serum from mice treated with 2 mg/kg FK506, but not mice treated with FKDC, potently inhibits T cell activation (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4E showing IL2 mRNA induction is inhibited by serum from FK506 but not FKDC treated mice

claim: Serum from mice treated with 2 mg/kg FK506 has higher serum levels of FK506 and causes systemic immunosuppression compared to mice treated with DC based FK506 delivery.
source: This is consistent with higher serum levels of FK506 and systemic immunosuppression in mice treated with conventional FK506 treatment compared to DC based FK506 delivery.
evidence: Inferred from T cell inhibition assay results in Figure 4E

claim: Amylase was increased in the systemic FK506 treatment group but not in the FKDC treatment group.
source: Amylase was increased in the systemic FK506 treatment group but not in the FKDC treatment group (Figure 4F).
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4F showing serum amylase levels in different treatment groups

claim: FK506 causes toxicity to the exocrine pancreas in rats.
source: This result is consistent with prior studies revealing toxicity to the exocrine pancreas in rats (Doi et al., 1992; Ito et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Doi et al., 1992; Ito et al., 1994

claim: In vivo transfer of antigen pulsed FKDC modulate immune outcomes in an antigen specific manner.
source: We conclude that in vivo transfer of antigen pulsed FKDC modulate immune outcomes in an antigen specific manner and protect from systemic immunosuppression and off target organ toxicity.
evidence: Demonstrated by multiple experiments in Figure 4 showing antigen-specific protection and reduced toxicity

claim: In vivo transfer of antigen pulsed FKDC protect from systemic immunosuppression and off target organ toxicity.
source: We conclude that in vivo transfer of antigen pulsed FKDC modulate immune outcomes in an antigen specific manner and protect from systemic immunosuppression and off target organ toxicity.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4E and 4F showing reduced systemic immunosuppression and toxicity with FKDC treatment

claim: The capacity of DCs to accumulate FK506 likely relates to their high expression of binding proteins such as FKBP12, which have high affinity for FK506.
source: The capacity of DCs to accumulate FK506 likely relates to their high expression of binding proteins such as FKBP12, which have high affinity for FK506 (Siekierka et al., 1989a).
evidence: Speculated based on expression data in Table 1 and supported by citation to Siekierka et al., 1989a

claim: T cells express high levels of FKBP12.
source: This suggestion is supported by the observation that T cells, which also express high levels of FKBP12, have the ability to concentrate radiolabeled FK506 500–1000 fold (Dumont et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dumont et al., 1994

claim: T cells have the ability to concentrate radiolabeled FK506 500–1000 fold.
source: This suggestion is supported by the observation that T cells, which also express high levels of FKBP12, have the ability to concentrate radiolabeled FK506 500–1000 fold (Dumont et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dumont et al., 1994

claim: The use of cellular drug sinks could be extended to other cell types with abundant FKBP expression.
source: These observations also suggest the possibility that the use of such cellular drug sinks could be extended to other cell types with abundant FKBP expression, or even extrapolated to other agents with analogous intracellular binding proteins.
evidence: Speculated based on the mechanism demonstrated in this study

claim: The use of cellular drug sinks could be extrapolated to other agents with analogous intracellular binding proteins.
source: These observations also suggest the possibility that the use of such cellular drug sinks could be extended to other cell types with abundant FKBP expression, or even extrapolated to other agents with analogous intracellular binding proteins.
evidence: Speculated based on the mechanism demonstrated in this study

claim: The actions of FKDC are potentially clinically relevant, as they prevent autoimmune arthritis in mice.
source: The actions of FKDC are potentially clinically relevant, as they prevent autoimmune arthritis in mice.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4A and 4B showing prevention of CIA in mice

claim: The lack of efficacy of FKDC loaded with irrelevant antigen indicates that the amount of drug delivered by FKDC is not by itself sufficient to elicit a systemic effect.
source: The lack of efficacy of FKDC loaded with irrelevant antigen indicates that the amount of drug delivered by FKDC is not by itself sufficient to elicit a systemic effect.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4A showing FKDC-CI did not protect mice from arthritis

claim: Upon encounter with antigen-specific FKDC, T cells initiate a program of activation but then undergo apoptosis.
source: Upon encounter with antigen-specific FKDC, T cells initiate a program of activation but then undergo apoptosis, explaining the antigen specific effect of FKDC transferred in vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro experiments in Figure 3 and inferred to explain in vivo results in Figure 4

claim: Systemic treatment of CIA with FK506 requires a minimum of 2 mg/kg or approximately 40 μg subcutaneously to elicit any therapeutic effect.
source: Systemic treatment of CIA with FK506 requires a minimum of 2 mg/kg or approximately 40 μg subcutaneously to elicit any therapeutic effect (Takagishi et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takagishi et al., 1989

claim: The dose delivered by 0.5 × 106 FKDC is a maximum of 5 ng.
source: In contrast, the amount of FK506 measured in culture supernatants (Figure 2B) predicts the dose delivered by 0.5 × 106 FKDC is a maximum of 5 ng
evidence: Calculated from FK506 ELISA measurements in Figure 2B

claim: 8000-fold less drug is required to elicit a therapeutic effect when delivered by a DC compared to systemic FK506 treatment.
source: this means 8000-fold less drug is required to elicit a therapeutic effect when delivered by a DC.
evidence: Calculated by comparing systemic FK506 dose (40 μg) to FKDC dose (5 ng)

claim: DC based drug delivery has the potential to limit adverse events by substantially limiting required doses by precisely targeting antigen specific T cells.
source: Since DC can be pulsed with antigen of interest prior to drug loading, DC based drug delivery has the potential to limit adverse events by substantially limiting required doses by precisely targeting antigen specific T cells.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing antigen-specific effects and reduced toxicity in Figures 4E and 4F

claim: Antigen-loaded DC have been widely used with excellent safety profiles.
source: Antigen-loaded DC have been widely used with excellent safety profiles (Sabado and Bhardwaj, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabado and Bhardwaj, 2010

claim: FK506 is a potent inhibitor of calcineurin, a phosphatase stimulated by T cell receptor signaling to regulate the transcription factor nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT).
source: FK506 is a potent inhibitor of calcineurin, a phosphatase stimulated by T cell receptor signaling to regulate the transcription factor nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT).
evidence: Established mechanism of FK506 action

claim: FK506 treated DC (FKDC) sequester and release the drug itself, at doses sufficient to block T cell activation.
source: Instead, we find that FK506 treated DC (FKDC) sequester and release the drug itself, at doses sufficient to block T cell activation, to target antigen specific immune responses and to prevent collagen induced arthritis in mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by multiple experiments in Figure 2 showing FK506 sequestration and release

claim: FKDC target antigen specific immune responses.
source: Instead, we find that FK506 treated DC (FKDC) sequester and release the drug itself, at doses sufficient to block T cell activation, to target antigen specific immune responses and to prevent collagen induced arthritis in mice.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4A showing antigen-specific protection from arthritis

claim: FKDC prevent collagen induced arthritis in mice.
source: Instead, we find that FK506 treated DC (FKDC) sequester and release the drug itself, at doses sufficient to block T cell activation, to target antigen specific immune responses and to prevent collagen induced arthritis in mice.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4A and 4B showing prevention of CIA

claim: DC can act as a biologic agent for drug delivery, with the potential to reduce drug dose and increase specificity in the treatment of autoimmune disease.
source: This demonstrates that DC can act as a biologic agent for drug delivery, with the potential to reduce drug dose and increase specificity in the treatment of autoimmune disease.
evidence: Inferred from all experimental results showing antigen-specific effects, reduced drug requirements, and decreased toxicity

claim: FK506 diffuses passively from FKDC.
source: We hypothesized that FK506 diffuses passively from FKDC, despite adequate washout from initial cultures.
evidence: Supported by experiments in Figure 2A showing no requirement for transcription, translation, or secretory pathway, and by FK506 measurements in Figure 2B

claim: Activated T cell death can be AICD-independent and regulated by bcl-2 family members.
source: Since activated T cell death can be AICD-independent (Hildeman et al., 2002) and regulated by bcl-2 family members, we examined this pathway.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hildeman et al., 2002
